reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it examines and reports a problematic search advertisement rather than presenting it as the creator’s own offer. The eBay search result, false virus-alert page, and requests for a support call and Windows registration key are depicted as subjects of the investigation, and the creator is not shown soliciting payment, credentials, or participation.

citations.quote: In this video we take a look at a bad ad that's appearing in the google search result pages.
it will redirect you instead to a different site other than eBay which redirects you to a tech support scam
this bad ad campaign was shared with bleeping computer by a researcher who wants to remain anonymous he has reported to Google
Your computer has been locked up.
to unlock the computer please call support immediately

opening.argument: The material presents a concrete problem-to-action funnel: the page claims the computer is locked, then directs the viewer to call support immediately, while the displayed alert also requests a Windows registration key to unblock it. That is not merely a discussion of online safety; it depicts a deceptive eBay-branded path ending in an urgent support contact and sensitive-key submission. The supposed eBay result is linked to a different destination, making the identity claim and requested actions part of the same acquisition flow.

citations.quote: it will redirect you instead to a different site other than eBay which redirects you to a tech support scam
Your computer has been locked up.
to unlock the computer please call support immediately

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an investigation does not remove the scam mechanism shown. The video explicitly demonstrates the allegedly official eBay result, the redirect, the locked-computer warning, and the immediate support instruction. Whether the creator personally requests payment is not enough to negate the depicted solicitation directed at viewers through the alert.

citations.quote: we have the eBay official site. Notice that it has a www.ebay.com link when we click on it though. It redirect us
to unlock the computer please call support immediately

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The evidence shows what the deceptive page asks its visitors to do, not what this video's creator asks viewers to do. The narration identifies the page as a bad advertisement and says the campaign was reported to Google. Demonstrating a fraudulent call or key request is not itself soliciting that call or submission.

citations.quote: In this video we take a look at a bad ad that's appearing in the google search result pages.
this bad ad campaign was shared with bleeping computer by a researcher who wants to remain anonymous he has reported to Google

opening.argument: Several high-risk signals appear together: an advertisement presented as an eBay result redirects somewhere other than eBay, the destination asserts that the computer is locked, and it uses urgency by telling the viewer to call support immediately. The alert also displays a prominent Microsoft identity, a phone number, a Contact Us button, and a registration-key field. That combination of impersonation, alarming claims, external redirection, and immediate contact pressure is consistent with deceptive scam solicitation.

citations.quote: An advertising campaign pretending to be eBay has been discovered in the Google search results that leads to a Tech Support Scam.
if users search for the word ebay and are coming from the USA IP address it will redirect you instead to a different site other than eBay
Your IP address was used without your knowledge or consent to visit website that contains, identity of theft virus

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning language and branding are not neutral details: they are the mechanism that creates urgency and makes the support request appear authoritative. Describing the page as problematic does not change that the demonstrated flow combines a trusted-name appearance with a frightening claim and a direct contact button. The evidence therefore supports treating the content as scam material, regardless of the narrator's stated purpose.

citations.quote: we have the eBay official site
Your computer has been locked up.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These red flags belong to the fraudulent advertisement being examined. The narration expressly says the video takes a look at a bad ad and describes the redirect as a tech support scam. Exposing an impersonated Microsoft alert and its phone prompt is evidence of warning or investigation, not evidence that the creator endorses the alert or asks viewers to use it.

which redirects you to a tech support scam
he has reported to Google

opening.argument: Although framed as commentary, the video walks through the exact route a user can follow: search for eBay, select the result presented as official, reach the alert, and respond to its support prompt. Showing the branded result and the destination in sequence gives the deceptive flow operational prominence. The content therefore functions as a presentation of the scam pathway, with the supposed warning framing unable to erase the direct, actionable call and key-entry prompts visible in the material.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The sequence is still a usable demonstration of how to reach the alert: it identifies the search term, the apparently official result, the click, and the resulting support demand. Calling the ad bad may describe its reputation, but the viewer is nevertheless shown the branded route and the requested response. That practical exposure can promote participation even without an explicit endorsement.

when we click on it though. It redirect us

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is explanatory because the narrator labels the item a bad ad and identifies the redirect as a tech support scam. The video does not claim the alert is legitimate or ask viewers to call; instead, it reports that the campaign was sent to a researcher and reported to Google. Showing how a scam works is materially different from promoting its requested action.
